title: Fireball over Douglas County, Washington, 2026 August 14 07:48 UTC: where its meteorites landed, predicted blind
question: Where do recovered meteorites of each mass lie on the ground, if any are found?

inputs.name: nasa_meo
inputs.terms: NASA Meteoroid Environment Office public event page (US Government work, no copyright in the US)

inputs.name: cneos
inputs.terms: NASA/JPL CNEOS fireball API (US Government data, public)

inputs.name: sounding
inputs.terms: NOAA NCEI IGRA2 (US Government data, public domain); Spokane WA, WMO 72786

inputs.name: elevation
inputs.terms: Open-Meteo elevation API (Copernicus DEM GLO-90; data CC BY 4.0, attribution)

method.blind_rule: stones released at the luminous end, plus at every fragmentation our own deceleration fit detects with a BIC gain of at least 10 (none was detected for Winchcombe, so the luminous end only); mass bins 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 160, 320 and 600 g; each find scored in the bin nearest its reported mass, against the 68% and 95% highest-density regions of that bin's simulated landing points

triage.rule: without a published speed profile alpha-beta cannot be fitted, so a weaker rule: a meteorite-dropping candidate needs (a) an entry speed of 20 km/s or less, (b) a published record of luminous flight at or below 35 km, and (c) an independent sign of surviving mass (a Doppler weather radar fall signature reported by the analysing agency); all three must hold

method.density_note: type unknown; ordinary chondrites are the most common falls
conflicts: CNEOS places peak brightness at 47.7, -119.4, 30.0 km; the camera line passes that latitude near 57 km, so the two records disagree on where the deep flight was; the camera solution (a triangulation) sets the end state, CNEOS only the triage
CNEOS velocity components have norm 22.9 km/s against its stated 12.2 km/s, so they are not used
method.track_record: on Winchcombe (2021) the same rule put 1 of 9 finds inside its 95% region: the simulated spread across the track was too narrow
limits: the published solution ends at the 45.5 km fragmentation at the published 14.6 km/s, so stones start there and lose no mass while they slow (the dark-flight model has no ablation); real stones shrink and slow sooner, so the regions are probably placed too far along the track
no speed profile is published: triage uses the simple rule, not alpha-beta, and no fragmentation fit is possible
position, height and angle errors are not published; they are assumed (2 km, 2 km, 3 degrees)
the satellite record (CNEOS) puts the deep flight about 40 km from the camera line; only the camera line is used
the meteorite type, and so its density (3500 kg/m^3 assumed), is unknown

prediction.frame: along/across the ground track from the end state (fireball_demo.along_cross)

scoring.rule: a hit when a recovered meteorite's reported find site lies inside the predicted 95% region of its mass bin (the bin nearest its reported mass); score after finds are published. Inside means fewer than 95% of that bin's stored landing points have a higher Gaussian kernel density (scipy gaussian_kde, default bandwidth, in metres along and across the track) than the find site (scripts/fireball_new.py score_find)
